stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I am implementing a C# application that combines POI candidates returned by multiple geocoding/search providers. For Google Places Text Search (New), I use a request ranked by RELEVANCE. Google returns the places in an ordered list, but I cannot find a public numeric relevance/matching score for each returned Place. I need to preserve the provider's own assessment of query relevance before candidates from different providers are processed by a common application-level scoring system. For example, if Google returns: result\[0\] = Place A result\[1\] = Place B result\[2\] = Place C I know that the order itself contains information, but I do not know whether it is valid to derive a numeric score from the position. My implementation question is therefore: 1. Is the result index guaranteed to represent decreasing query relevance when Text Search (New) uses RELEVANCE ranking? 2. Can the result position safely be used as an application-side relevance signal? 3. If yes, is there any documented relationship between consecutive ranks that would justify a numeric conversion such as: rank 1 -\> 100 rank 2 -\> 95 rank 3 -\> 90 or must the ranking be treated as ordinal only? 4. Is there another field in the Places Text Search (New) response that should be used instead to represent query-match relevance? I am not trying to reproduce Google's ranking algorithm. I need to know what part of the public API contract can safely be used when implementing an application-side scoring algorithm. waiting for your response Regards

I understand how that works with insertions since inserting into a skipfield will, at worst, create another block, not reallocating any existing blocks. However, how does this work with erasure. If you currently have an iterator to index 42 and someone deletes it, the element may still be there physically in the block (marked as erased) but any attempt to dereference that iterator is going to be problematic, yes? Even worse where the erasure is for the last item in a block and the block itself disappears totally. In that case, both dereferencing and attempting to advance to the next item seems to be likely to cause an issue. Or does each block/element have to remember all iterators that are currently active on it to prevent these issues? The first case could probably be handled by using std::optional types to store the elements so that dereferencing could catch erasures after the iterator was set (for example, causing an exception or auto-magically advancing the iterator to the next unerased element). But I'm not sure how entire block deletions could work in that case.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: MySQL fails to complete initialization when starting on NFS storage
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: When MySQL starts on NFS storage, the NFS server does not respond to the `openat` system call, causing the worker threads to enter state D (uninterruptible sleep). The main thread times out while waiting on the futex, and the service ultimately hangs during the “InnoDB initialization” phase. Below is the analysis provided by the AI: mysqld thread states: tid=68418 state=D wchan=rpc_wait_bit_killable syscall=257(openat) tid=7867 state=S wchan=futex_wait ← The main thread is waiting for the one above The worker thread is stuck on the `openat` (open file) system call. `wchan=rpc_wait_bit_killable` indicates that the NFS client is waiting for an OPEN RPC response from the NFS server—in other words, `mysqld` is attempting to open an InnoDB file (one of `redo`, `dblwr`, or `undo`), but the NFS server has not responded to this OPEN call, causing the thread to hang in state D. The main thread is waiting for it via a futex, so the entire mysqld process is stuck at “InnoDB initialization.” This is my first time encountering this issue. I’d like to know how to fix it and if there are any good solutions. Would iSCSI be a better option?

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Why does TypeScript lose the correlation between a discriminant and a generic payload?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I have a discriminated union where the relationship between type and payload is preserved when I work directly with the union: type Message = | { type: "text"; payload: string } | { type: "count"; payload: number }; function handle(message: Message) { if (message.type === "text") { message.payload.toUpperCase(); } if (message.type === "count") { message.payload.toFixed(); } } However, when I try to express the same relationship through generics, TypeScript no longer seems to preserve the correlation: type MessageMap = { text: string; count: number; }; function handle<K extends keyof MessageMap>( type: K, payload: MessageMap[K] ) { if (type === "text") { payload.toUpperCase(); } } The call site is type-safe, but inside the generic function type === "text" doesn't narrow payload to string . Why can't TypeScript use the relationship between K and MessageMap[K] for control-flow narrowing? Is there a type design that preserves this correlation without manually converting the generic into a discriminated union?
